children: Shristi Achar Bengaluru: Subcontracting costs are rising for Indian IT services companies, as demand for AI and other specialist skills outpaces internal hiring and training, while uncertain project pipelines make firms wary of adding permanent employees. Subcontractor costs as a share of revenue increased sequentially at most firms in the June quarter, Kotak Institutional Equities said in a note.

The ratio rose to 9.6% at LTM from 8.3% in March, to 15.5% from 15.3% at Persistent Systems, to 11.7% from 11.5% at Wipro and to 8.7% from 8.5% at Infosys. Tata Consultancy Services and Tech Mahindra recorded marginal declines, while HCLTech posted flat subcontracting costs at 14.8% of revenue.

Data for the last 10 quarters for top IT service firms show that this cost has been increasing 10-20 basis points (0.1-0.2 percentage points) on average every quarter, as they increasingly engaged freelancers and independent agencies to carry out project work. External specialists generally cost more for companies than their own employees and increase the pressure on their margins.

Beyond reduced reliance on H-1B visa workers, the data reflect a gap between skills available within IT companies and those required by clients. Demand is growing for AI engineering, data engineering, cybersecurity, cloud modernisation and employees who can work directly with clients to deploy AI systems. "The biggest driver is that the skills clients are demanding are changing faster than the providers can rebuild their permanent workforces," said Phil Fersht, CEO of HFS Research. "Providers cannot afford to keep all of that expensive talent permanently on the bench, so subcontracting becomes the pressure valve." Uncertain demand is also influencing staffing decisions. Clients want projects to start quickly, but service providers have limited visibility on whether the work will continue for several years.

Hiring contractors for six or 12 months can therefore carry less risk than adding permanent employees who may later remain unutilised, Fersht said. India currently has about 420,000 AI professionals against an estimated demand of 600,000-650,000, said Neeti Sharma, chief executive of staffing services company TeamLease Digital. The shortage is particularly evident in generative AI, machine learning operations, AI engineering and data orchestration. "Companies themselves are not yet sure what long-term AI talent requirements will look like. The technology is evolving very quickly, and skills that are critical today could change in a couple of years," Sharma said.

title: Top IT's Subcontractor Costs Creep Up as Volatile Pipelines Force Flexible Staffing
